children: By Bill Peters
GameStop's base of fervent retail investors is still intact, but Needham analysts say more institutional investors should take note of the company's transformation
Shares of GameStop are up around 36.5% so far this year.
The trading-card boom has bailed out GameStop, and some mainstream investors are ignoring it at their own risk, Needham analysts said on Tuesday.

The Needham team of Stefanos Crist and Bernie McTernan became the latest analysts to find renewed faith in the videogame and collectibles chain and original meme stock. They started coverage of GameStop shares (GME) with a buy rating and a $33 price target.
"We think the company's meme history has been a disqualifier for institutional investors, who are overlooking a much leaner company with growth potential in new end markets," they wrote.

One of those areas is collectibles and trading cards, which has boomed thanks to the pandemic as well as the convergence of nostalgia with expanding financialization. Needham estimates the market for sports cards and cards used in games - like Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering - could reach $45 billion by 2031. While GameStop's videogame business has struggled to keep up with the rise of digital gaming, collectibles now make up 45% of the retailer's revenue overall.
"The shift of focus to collectibles effectively saved the company," the analysts said.

Some have seen GameStop's waves of store closures over recent years - it has shrunk its store count to around 1,900 from roughly 5,500 since 2019 - as a sign of an inevitable demise. But the Needham analysts noted that every store is now profitable. At the end of the second quarter, GameStop had around $5 billion in cash.
Shares of GameStop were up 0.4% on Tuesday. The stock is up around 36.5% so far this year.

In recent weeks, other analysts have come around to GameStop after the meme-stock fervor and previous stretch of losses had scared them away. Those who cover the stock now generally think GameStop's financials are on more solid footing. They've also argued that meme traders have looked elsewhere for risky bets, including in crypto and prediction markets.

Still, GameStop offers online pack rips, where collectors can open a pack of cards virtually, see what cards or other items they get, keep the ones they like and sell back the others. They can potentially get higher-value fare in higher-priced packs. That segment of GameStop's business lists "chase" items - or rare, coveted items - such as Pokemon cards and even Rolex watches worth more than $60,000.
"We think there is significant overlap between consumers who bet on sports and customers who like sports and trading cards," the Needham analysts wrote.
The analysts said that while GameStop doesn't offer so-called live selling - or live-streamed auctions where trading cards and others can sell in a matter of seconds - it could in the future.

Analysts broadly have questioned GameStop's interest in buying or collaborating with eBay (EBAY). But the Needham analysts said the two companies' interests align in several ways. They noted that GameStop in 2024 partnered with Professional Sports Authenticator, which authenticates cards and collectibles, and which also partners with eBay. EBay in 2022 also bought TCG Player, an online marketplace and price tracker for trading cards used in games like Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering.

As competition heats up in trading cards, the analysts said GameStop's size gives it an advantage, as its "network and scale provides better pricing from card distributors, more inventory for repacks, and a large consumer base [and] distribution network for reselling cards," they said. "GameStop also sells other collectibles including action figures, clothing and other accessories that cater to a similar audience as trading cards," they added.
The Needham analysts noted that the retail-investor base that has carried GameStop's stock over the past five years is still intact.

"We think the company has become more institutionally relevant now that its retail business has been cleaned up and the collectibles business is driving more meaningful revenue," they wrote. "However, we think there is more retail ownership than other companies in our coverage and this could drive volatility in shares."
-Bill Peters
